# Actual Test
- After the MD was finished, I turned on the compensator and made sure it behaved as expected.
- No corrections were applied initially as the field was already at acceptable levels.
- Dwane played a single LHC SC at about 18:57, which immediately pushed the magnets to the hysteretic state
- Moved back to SFT. The compensator fixed the drift
	- There was still a loss alarm, although usually this happens several times after SC change, and this time it only happened once.
- I observed that the effSpillLength drifted and sharing error improved and held steady
	- This is the contrary of in [[06-05-26 MD - Magnetic Calibration, Flat-top Studies]]. There, in the static case of the LHC SC, we saw that the dipole correction fixed the spill length properly but not the sharing factor.
- When we tried with SFT->LHC in the MD, the effSpillLength was fixed and the sharing error was still off
- When we look at a normal LHC->SFT change, both factors drift
- Weird note: sharing error increased when they switched to longer flat-bottom (HIRADMAT1 -> HIRADMAT2)

# Email Update

Hello everyone,

This is an update on the testing of the hysteresis drift compensator.

Brief summary: After a supercycle change in the SPS, the spill quality and sharing accuracy decrease. During an MD on the 6th of May, we showed that these parameters could largely be recovered by simply trimming the flat-top dipole field (i.e. SPSBEAM/B) to account for the effect of hysteresis. We tried this on an SFT->LHC change, which is the simpler case because there the hysteretic field is a static offset. However, we actually wanted to compensate for the slow drift of the flat-top field observed when switching from LHC->SFT, as this happens over several hours and is generally dealt with by several manual tune trims. I developed a simple feed-forward drift compensator on UCAP which measures the field at a fixed point on the flat-top, finds the delta from what it's meant to be, and then trims the SPSBEAM/BHYS parameter accordingly to compensate for the hysteretic effect on the next cycle. Slides attached for more details on all this[^1].

I tested the compensator on 23rd June without beam and on 16th July with beam. The first test proved that the many safeguards worked and that the dipole field drift could be mostly eliminated, although there was a slight time-lag due to the one-cycle feed-forward.

During the second test on the 16th, I turned on the compensator during SFT physics. Dwane kindly played a single LHC filling supercycle which established the hysteresis, and went back to SFT. The compensator worked nicely to counteract the slow drift. Below you can see the effect on the flat-top field (blue) and the current to the MBIs (top magenta). Bear in mind that each point on the graph is one SFTPRO1 flat-top with the relevant quantity measured at a reference point mid-way through the flat-top. Grey background is SFT physics, the single white column is the one LHC filling SC played.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Although the field was compensated nicely, the spill quality (orange) and sharing error (green) acted contrary to expectations from the MD. In the MD, the spill quality was immediately restored by the flat-top compensation (see slides), whereas here it seems to drift as if no correction were applied. Likewise in the MD, the sharing accuracy was not entirely fixed by the trim, but here it is restored to pre-LHC levels. Eventually Dwane got a call from the NA complaining about the spill so we turned off the compensation and he did a tune trim to restore the spill (around 19:08 on plot). There was a single cycle without dipole compensation or tune trims, at which point the spill length remained unchanged but the sharing accuracy worsened. So, to summarise, the compensator fixed the quantity we didn't expect it to, and had no effect on the expected quantity. Maybe the batteries of the UCAP device are in the wrong way round.

The difference probably lies in some hysteretic difference between the LHC filling SC (as during the MD) and SFT physics SC (this recent test). First thought would be that this is a tune effect, but QH and QV are actually remarkably stable when compensating the dipole B, both during the MD and during the compensator testing (at least as far as we can measure them, i.e. up until the actual start of the extraction). I am working on some analysis of the orbits at the moment and will produce a more complete write-up later, but if anyone has any ideas, I would be interested to hear them.

@Francesco Maria Velotti Now that SFTPRO1 is about to stop, can you think of any way we can continue to develop this using the ion cycles? This mostly depends on if the extraction there is similar enough to the SFTPRO1 slow extraction and how sensitive it would be to these same effects.

@Kevin Shing Bruce Li Whilst looking at the BBQ signal during extraction for the MD, we noticed a very static peak around 0.65. Do you have any idea what this could be? The first assumption was the damper but we thought this was off during the MD[^2].

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Best,

Brendan
